title: Credit arbitration resolution bypass allows buyer to cancel arbitration against themselves
description: The `resolveArbitration` method allows both the buyer and the seller to resolve a credit arbitration with resolution='cancelled'. When a credit arbitration is triggered (due to a buyer defaulting on a balance payment after the deadline), the buyer (debtor) can call `PATCH /marketplace/arbitrations/:id/resolve` with `{resolution: 'cancelled'}` to mark the arbitration as resolved. Unlike `defaulted` (which calls `creditScore.recordDefault`) or `paid_late` (which calls `creditScore.recordLatePayment`), the `cancelled` resolution applies NO credit score penalty. The offer remains in `arbitration` status but the arbitration record itself is marked as resolved, effectively neutralizing the enforcement mechanism.
impact: A defaulting buyer can evade credit score penalties and the entire arbitration enforcement mechanism by self-resolving the arbitration as 'cancelled'. This undermines the credit system's trust model and allows repeat offenders to maintain clean credit scores while defaulting on balance payments.
attack_path: 1. Buyer makes credit offer with advance + balance terms. 2. Seller accepts; advance is paid via escrow. 3. After weight validation, balance becomes due. 4. Buyer does not pay balance within deadline. 5. System triggers arbitration (cron job sets offer to 'arbitration' status, creates CreditArbitration record). 6. Buyer calls `PATCH /api/v1/marketplace/arbitrations/:arbitrationId/resolve` with `{"resolution": "cancelled"}`. 7. Arbitration is marked resolved with no credit score penalty. 8. Buyer repeats with other sellers.
evidence: File: credit-offers.service.ts, lines 712-717: access check allows both buyer and seller (`row.sellerUserId !== user.id && row.buyerUserId !== user.id`). Lines 778-787: the `cancelled` resolution branch has NO role check (unlike `paid_late` and `defaulted` which check `row.sellerUserId !== user.id`) and applies no credit score penalty.
remediation: Add a role check to the `cancelled` resolution branch: only the seller should be able to cancel an arbitration, as the seller is the aggrieved party. Alternatively, if both parties should be allowed to cancel, add a credit score impact for buyer-initiated cancellations. Suggested fix: add `if (row.buyerUserId === user.id) { throw new ForbiddenException('Seul le vendeur peut annuler un arbitrage'); }` before the `cancelled` resolution handling on line 778.

title: Any user can trigger AI moderation and potential removal of any community post
description: The `POST /feed/moderate` endpoint allows any authenticated user with an active profile to submit any post ID for AI moderation review. The `moderatePostAsync` method fetches the post by ID without checking whether the calling user is the author, an admin, or has any relationship to the post. If the AI flags the content as a violation with `actionRecommended: 'remove'`, the post is immediately marked as `isRemoved: true`. Additionally, the violation sanction is incorrectly attributed to the reporting user (`userId` parameter) rather than the post author (`post.authorUserId`), meaning a reporter could accumulate sanctions against themselves or cause incorrect sanction records.
impact: A malicious user can repeatedly trigger AI moderation on any post they want removed. If the AI classifier has any false-positive rate, an attacker can systematically target legitimate posts for removal. The misattribution of sanctions (to reporter instead of author) could be weaponized in two ways: (1) generating false violation records attributed to innocent users, (2) the actual violating content author escapes sanctions.
attack_path: 1. Attacker authenticates and obtains a valid active profile. 2. Attacker discovers or enumerates post IDs (e.g., from GET /feed/posts). 3. Attacker calls `POST /api/v1/feed/moderate` with `{"postId": "<target-post-id>"}` repeatedly. 4. AI moderation reviews the post content. If the content is borderline or the AI produces a false positive, the post is automatically removed. 5. The violation sanction is recorded against the attacker's userId (not the post author), creating incorrect audit records.
evidence: Controller: community-feed.controller.ts line 96-101: `moderatePost(@CurrentUser() user: User, @Body() dto: PostSendModerateDto) { return this.feed.moderatePostAsync(dto.postId, user.id); }`. Service: community-feed.service.ts line 536-544: `moderatePostAsync` fetches post by ID with no ownership check. Line 543: passes `userId` (reporter) to `reviewPostAsync`. Line 730-737: post can be removed by AI. Line 741-743: `recordViolation` called with reporter's `userId` instead of `post.authorUserId`.
remediation: 1. Remove or restrict the `POST /feed/moderate` endpoint. If it's meant as a user reporting mechanism, rename it and add rate limiting per user-post pair to prevent abuse. 2. Fix the userId attribution in `moderatePostAsync`: pass `post.authorUserId` to `reviewPostAsync` instead of the reporter's userId, so sanctions are correctly attributed to the content author. 3. Consider requiring admin privileges for triggering moderation, or implementing a separate report queue that doesn't immediately trigger AI review and removal.

title: Banned user path exemption uses exact match allowing bypass via trailing slash or query params
description: The `SupabaseJwtGuard` uses `req.path` with exact Set lookup (`ACCOUNT_STATUS_EXEMPT_PATHS.has(path)`) to determine whether a banned/suspended user should be allowed through. The exempt paths are: `/api/v1/auth/me`, `/api/v1/health`, `/api/v1/config/client`. The use of `req.path` (which does not include query parameters) is correct for query param bypasses. However, framework-level path normalization inconsistencies between Express and NestJS route matching could potentially allow a banned user to reach non-exempt endpoints. More critically, the `/api/v1/auth/me` exemption opens access to the full auth controller including `DELETE /api/v1/auth/me/account` (account deletion), `PATCH /api/v1/auth/me/profile`, and notification management endpoints, since the exempt path check only compares `req.path` to `/api/v1/auth/me` (exact match), while these sub-routes have different paths like `/api/v1/auth/me/account`.
impact: A banned user retains the ability to: (1) read their profile info via GET /auth/me (intended), (2) read client config (intended), (3) read health endpoint (intended). The current implementation correctly blocks sub-paths under /auth/me since they don't match the exact string. The primary risk is if the path comparison can be bypassed through encoding tricks or framework normalization to reach other endpoints while banned. However, upon deep analysis, Express normalizes req.path before it reaches the guard, making this attack difficult in practice. Severity reduced to MEDIUM as the implementation is fragile but not currently exploitable in standard Express configurations.
attack_path: 1. User's account is banned by admin. 2. User still has valid JWT (Supabase tokens don't expire immediately upon ban). 3. User attempts to access endpoints. 4. SupabaseJwtGuard checks `req.path` against exempt set. 5. Standard sub-paths under /auth/me/ (like /auth/me/account) are correctly blocked because they don't exactly match '/api/v1/auth/me'. 6. However, path normalization edge cases (double slashes, encoded characters) could potentially cause `req.path` to not match the exact exempt path, which would actually improve security (blocking the user from even the exempt paths). The fragility works both ways.
evidence: File: supabase-jwt.guard.ts, lines 16-20: `const ACCOUNT_STATUS_EXEMPT_PATHS = new Set(['/api/v1/auth/me', '/api/v1/health', '/api/v1/config/client'])`. Line 38-39: `const path = req.path; if (!ACCOUNT_STATUS_EXEMPT_PATHS.has(path))`. Auth controller at auth.controller.ts shows sub-routes under /auth/me/* that correctly would NOT match the exempt path.
remediation: Use `startsWith` matching instead of exact match for intentionally exempt path prefixes, and explicitly enumerate all sub-paths that should be exempt. Alternatively, use route-level decorators/metadata to mark endpoints as banned-user-accessible rather than relying on string path matching. Also consider adding a comment documenting the security intent of each exempt path.

title: Vet appointment cancellation role determination uses getById which returns data to unauthorized users before checking role
description: The `cancel` endpoint on `VetAppointmentController` first calls `this.appointments.getById(user, id)` to determine whether the user is the vet or the producer, then dispatches to `cancelByVet` or `cancelByProducer` accordingly. The `getById` method (line 760-774 of vet-appointment.service.ts) fetches the full appointment data including farm details, producer info, vet info, financial data (servicePrice, blockedAmount), and the visit report, and returns it if the user is either the producer or the vet. However, the cancellation method then calls `getById` again at the end. The primary issue is that the role check at lines 177 is based on comparing `r.vetUserId === user.id`, but `r` contains the full mapped row response. If `getById` returns before the `cancelByVet`/`cancelByProducer` method's own ownership validation runs, the response leaks appointment details. In practice, `getById` already performs the access check (line 771), so this is actually safe, but the pattern is fragile.
impact: Currently not exploitable because `getById` correctly checks `row.producerUserId !== user.id && row.vetUserId !== user.id` and throws ForbiddenException. However, the pattern of fetching data to determine authorization role is an anti-pattern that could lead to future bugs if `getById` logic changes.
attack_path: Not currently exploitable. The `getById` method correctly validates access. However: 1. User A (neither vet nor producer for appointment X) calls `POST /api/v1/vet-appointments/:x/cancel`. 2. `getById` throws ForbiddenException. 3. No cancellation occurs.
evidence: Controller: vet-appointment.controller.ts lines 170-181. Service: vet-appointment.service.ts lines 760-774 (getById with access check).
remediation: Refactor the cancel endpoint to use the `requireVetAppointment` or `requireProducerAppointment` helper methods directly rather than calling `getById` for role determination. This makes the security intent explicit and avoids returning full appointment data before the authorization decision is made.

title: Moderation violation sanctions attributed to wrong user (reporter instead of author)
description: When any user calls `POST /feed/moderate`, the `moderatePostAsync(postId, userId)` method receives the reporter's userId. This userId is then passed to `reviewPostAsync`, which calls `sanctions.recordViolation({ userId, ... })`. The `userId` here is the reporting user, NOT the post author (`post.authorUserId`). This means sanctions and violations from user-triggered moderation are recorded against the wrong user. For internally-triggered calls (e.g., from `createPost`), the userId IS the author, so those work correctly.
impact: Moderation sanctions from user-triggered reviews are attributed to the reporter, not the content author. This corrupts the sanction/violation database, potentially leading to incorrect community bans. An attacker could theoretically exploit this to generate violation records against targeted users by having them report posts (social engineering), though the more direct impact is incorrect enforcement.
attack_path: 1. User A creates a post with borderline content. 2. User B reports the post via `POST /feed/moderate` with `{"postId": "<post-by-A>"}`. 3. AI flags the content as a violation. 4. The violation sanction is recorded against User B (the reporter), not User A (the author). 5. If User B reports multiple flagged posts, they accumulate violations and may be banned from the feed themselves.
evidence: community-feed.controller.ts line 96-101: passes `user.id` (reporter). community-feed.service.ts line 543: `reviewPostAsync(postId, post.body, userId)` where userId is the reporter. Line 741-743: `recordViolation({ userId, ... })` uses the reporter's ID.
remediation: In `moderatePostAsync`, pass `post.authorUserId` instead of the caller's `userId` to `reviewPostAsync`. Change line 543 from `await this.reviewPostAsync(postId, post.body, userId)` to `await this.reviewPostAsync(postId, post.body, post.authorUserId)`. This ensures the content author receives the violation, not the reporting user.
